messages.author: fc22cb727156ff4f
messages.subject: Performance of summarise (and plyr)
parts:
Hi,

Just today I was reading about the recent optimization work of Hadley
on plyr and was trying things on a big dataset of mine. I remarked the
following, although with plyr commit a35337d72618607096 because I
could not install the freshest: 'split-indices.r' was missing from
Collate and adding it caused issues down the line with C stuff. So
those C optimizations are not taken in account here.

library(plyr)

# let's build a dataset
n <- 10^6
ng <- 60
X <- data.frame(a=cut(runif(n),
breaks=seq(0,1,length.out=ng+1)),
x=runif(n), y=runif(n), z=rnorm(n))

Now compare summarise() with a function returning a named vector (the
result of both constructions is the same):

system.time(ddply(X, ~a, function(Y) {
c(
s1=mean(Y$x),
s2=mean(Y$y),
s3=mean(Y$y) + sum(Y$z)
)
}))
user system elapsed
1.519 0.418 1.949

system.time(ddply(X, ~a, summarise,
s1=mean(x),
s2=mean(y),
s3=mean(y) + sum(z)
))
user system elapsed
1.568 0.437 2.018

= Virtually no difference

Now use a list rather than a data.frame that has to be split

XL <- split(X, X$a)

system.time(ldply(XL, function(Y) {
c(
s1=mean(Y$x),
s2=mean(Y$y),
s3=mean(Y$y) + sum(Y$z)
)
}))
user system elapsed
0.019 0.000 0.020

system.time(ldply(XL, summarise,
s1=mean(x),
s2=mean(y),
s3=mean(y) + sum(z)
))
user system elapsed
0.070 0.000 0.073

First, the computation is much faster, which is to be expected since
there is one less step (the splitting) to be done (but see
post-scriptum). But, what is more surprising: summarise is much slower
than the function(Y) construct. The times are small here but
increasing the size of the data shows this just as clearly. I don't
understand what is going on within plyr's insides but this might be a
lead to follow for optimization.

PS: I also tried to include the time to split the data.frame in the
system.time call.

foo <- function() {
XL <- split(X, X$a)
ldply(XL, summarise,
s1=mean(x),
s2=mean(y),
s3=mean(y) + sum(z)
)
}
system.time(foo())
user system elapsed
0.491 0.303 0.798

so it seems that ddply is three times slower than split+ldply (1.519 >
0.491). But maybe this has been solved by the C stuff.

JiHO

Summarise is so much slower because it has to create a data frame.
Next on my list of things to look at is ways to improve this. So far
I've been focussing on the splitting and iterating, not the processing
and combining.

messages.subject: Re: Performance of summarise (and plyr)
parts:
Oh and split-indices isn't missing, but I forgot to add it to the
package collation. With my new devtools package, I should pick up on
these problems earlier, so the development package is more likely to
run successfully.

And here's a benchmark that illustrates best what I've been working on
- big savings when you're processing large data sets with many groups.
I should have the code that powers this up by the end of the day.
Working on documentation now and then I'll merge in the topic branch

n <- 10^6
X <- data.frame(
a = sample(60, n, rep = T),
b = sample(1000, n, rep = T),
x=runif(n), y=runif(n), z=rnorm(n)
)
iX <- idata.frame(X)

f <- function(Y) {

c(
s1=mean(Y$x),
s2=mean(Y$y),
s3=mean(Y$y) + sum(Y$z)
)
}

# Small number of groups
system.time(a <- dlply(X, ~a, f))
system.time(b <- dlply(idata.frame(X), ~a, f))
system.time({
lX <- split(X, X$a)
c <- llply(lX, f)
names(c)[1] <- "a"
})

# Large number of groups
system.time(a <- dlply(X, ~b, f))
system.time(b <- dlply(iX, ~b, f))
system.time({
lX <- split(X, X$b)
c <- ldply(lX, f)
names(c)[1] <- "a"
})


Hadley

dlply is now on par with split for data frames, and about 2x-5x faster
when you use immutable data frames.

messages.subject: Re: Performance of summarise (and plyr)
parts:
> idata.frame is something new in plyr? I cannot find mention of it
> anywhere. I guess that the difference is that the data.frame cannot be
> altered ("immutable") but plyr never does, as far as I understand (it
> works on it and returns a *new* data.frame).

Yes, it's new, and it brings big performance improvements because
subsetting creates a reference to the origin dataset, instead of
copying the contents into a new one.

> If so, does that mean
> that they could become default in all d*ply functions? That would be
> really cool given the speed improvements you show here!

Eventually, but currently I want to leave it optional because there
are probably some data.frame features that I haven't captured
perfectly in idata.frames.
